records.old:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) classify materials as conductors, insulators, semiconductors and superconductors based on their electrical properties,
b) describe intrinsic and extrinsic (n-type and p-type) semiconductors,
c) explain how doping and temperature change the conductivity of semiconductors,
d) explain the special properties and uses of superconductors,
e) relate the properties of these materials to their applications in household wiring, solar panels, microchips and MRI machines,
f) appreciate the role of electronics in Kenya's technological growth and renewable energy.
records.new:
By the end of the sub strand, the learner should be able to:
a) explain the meaning of insulator, conductor, semiconductor and superconductor,
b) distinguish between insulators, conductors, semiconductors and superconductors,
c) investigate the electrical behaviour of conductors, semiconductors and insulators with varying temperatures,
d) explain intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors as used in Physics,
e) explain the formation of n-type and p-type semiconductors from intrinsic semiconductors,
f) describe the applications of conductors, semiconductors, insulators and superconductors in day-to-day life,
g) appreciate the applications of conductors, semiconductors, insulators and superconductors in day-to-day life.
records.why: The unit listed six outcomes in its own words (for example an outcome about doping and temperature, and one about Kenya's technological growth). KICD March 2025 lists seven specific learning outcomes, a) to g), and they must be quoted word for word. Every lesson still serves them: a, b in Lessons 1, 2 and 6; c in Lesson 3 (temperature) and Lesson 6; d, e in Lessons 3 and 4; f, g in Lesson 7.
records.group_headline: Unit text now matches KICD March 2025 wording: 7 learning outcomes, content list, 2 key inquiry questions, core competencies, values and PCIs (the unit had paraphrased or different versions)

records.old: Then she warms the diode in a sealed bag in hand-hot water while students watch the bulb and observe a small change. Students record what they see.
records.new: Then she warms the diode in a sealed bag in hand-hot water while students watch the bulb; they will probably see little or no change and should record exactly that (a diode is a doped device, not a pure-silicon sample, and a torch bulb cannot show a change this small). If a digital multimeter and an NTC thermistor (for example from an old electronic thermometer or charger) are available, use them for the same warming step: on the resistance range the reading falls clearly as the thermistor warms, which shows the semiconductor trend directly.
records.why: Warming a forward-biased diode by about 25 K lowers its forward voltage by only about 2 mV per K, about 50 mV out of 3 V (about 2 percent change in a bulb current near 0.15 A), so no bulb change can be seen, and the diode is a doped p-n device, not pure silicon. So the lesson's 'small change' was not a realistic observation and did not test the trend. KICD outcome c asks learners to investigate behaviour with varying temperatures, so a thermistor (a semiconducting material whose resistance falls with temperature; a typical 10 kilo-ohm one goes from about 10 to about 5 kilo-ohm between 25 C and 40 C, checked as 10 x exp(3950 x (1/313 - 1/298)) = about 5.3) is offered as a measurable option. Teacher decides whether such parts are available locally.
records.group_headline: Warming a diode cannot show the semiconductor temperature trend with a bulb (change about 2 percent); the lesson now says so and offers a thermistor and multimeter if available, plus real temperature data
records.reference: Sedra and Smith, Microelectronic Circuits (diode forward voltage falls about 2 mV per K); Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics (NTC thermistors)

records.old: Be honest that a torch bulb is a crude detector and a small change may be hard to see; say: 'A bulb is not sensitive, so we use the dataset to see the trend clearly.'
records.new: Be honest that a torch bulb is a crude detector and a diode is not a pure-silicon sample, so you expect little or no change; say: 'A bulb is not sensitive, so we use the dataset to see the trend clearly.' If you use a thermistor, ask: 'What happens to the resistance when it warms? Is that like copper or different?'

records.old: Part C: Groups analyse a temperature dataset for pure silicon, showing resistivity falling as temperature rises, and a copper dataset showing resistance rising slightly with temperature.
records.new: Part C: Groups analyse a temperature dataset for pure silicon (resistivity about 2300 ohm metre at 300 K, about 600 at 320 K, about 180 at 340 K) and a copper dataset (about 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre at 300 K, about 1.8 x 10^-8 at 320 K, about 2.0 x 10^-8 at 340 K), showing silicon's resistivity falling steeply as temperature rises and copper's rising slightly.
records.why: The lesson refers to a temperature dataset but never supplies one, so a teacher could not run Part C tomorrow. Values supplied are approximate model values I calculated and checked twice: for pure silicon, carrier number grows as T^1.5 x exp(-Eg/2kT) with Eg = 1.12 eV, giving conductivity about 3.9 times higher at 320 K and about 12.8 times higher at 340 K (carrier mobility falling as T^-1.5 reduces this slightly), so resistivity 2300 -> about 590 -> about 180. For copper, resistivity rises about 0.39 percent per K (temperature coefficient 0.0039 per K): +7.8 percent at 320 K (1.83 x 10^-8) and +15.6 percent at 340 K (1.97 x 10^-8). Teachers may replace them with measured or textbook data.
records.reference: Sze and Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices (intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon); CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (resistivity and temperature coefficient of copper)

records.old: What did the simulation show when we changed the energy gap (metal 0 eV, germanium 0.67 eV, silicon 1.1 eV, insulator above about 5 eV), raised the temperature of silicon, and added phosphorus or boron? Record the numbers and the number of free electrons and holes you saw.
records.new: In the simulation we changed one variable at a time. Gap: a metal (0 eV) gave a high current reading, germanium (0.67 eV) and silicon (1.1 eV) gave a few free electrons, and an insulator (above about 5 eV) gave almost none. Warming silicon freed more electrons and holes. Adding phosphorus gave extra free electrons (n-type) and adding boron gave holes (p-type), and the doped silicon stayed electrically neutral overall.
records.why: Lesson 5's summary table entries were questions to answer, while Lessons 1 to 4, 6 and 7 give completed statements that feed the Final Explanation. Rewritten as completed entries based on the lesson's own expected results so the table can be used to build the final explanation.
records.group_headline: Lesson 5 Summary Table was a list of questions, unlike every other lesson; it now holds the completed expected entries

records.old: What did the simulation evidence tell us about how well our band model works? Which parts did it support, which parts did we have to change, and what are the limits of a simulation compared with the real bulb test in the Nairobi wiring circuit?
records.new: The simulation supported the band model: the size of the energy gap controls how many electrons can move, silicon and germanium conduct a little and more when warmer, and doping raises conduction in a controlled way. We changed our model to show the four gaps side by side, more free electrons and holes at higher temperature, and neutral doped silicon. A simulation simplifies real atoms and cannot show the bulb or the 3 V cells, so it supports a model but does not replace the bulb test.
records.why: Lesson 5's summary table entries were questions to answer, while Lessons 1 to 4, 6 and 7 give completed statements that feed the Final Explanation. Rewritten as completed entries based on the lesson's own expected results so the table can be used to build the final explanation.

records.old: Using the evidence, explain why copper lights the bulb while glass, wood and plastic almost do not, why silicon sits in between and conducts more when warmer, and how phosphorus (n-type) and boron (p-type) change it. Link your answer to why Mr Otieno can safely hold PVC-covered copper cable.
records.new: Copper lights the bulb because its bands overlap (gap 0 eV), so electrons move easily. Glass, wood and plastic almost do not, because the gap is above about 5 eV and almost no electrons can move, which is why Mr Otieno can safely hold PVC-covered copper cable. Silicon sits in between and conducts more when warmer, and phosphorus (n-type) or boron (p-type) change its conduction in a controlled way.
records.why: Lesson 5's summary table entries were questions to answer, while Lessons 1 to 4, 6 and 7 give completed statements that feed the Final Explanation. Rewritten as completed entries based on the lesson's own expected results so the table can be used to build the final explanation.

records.old: We say almost none, not zero.'
records.new: We say almost none, not zero.' Language support: write each new word on the board with a Kiswahili term beside it (suggested: conductor = kondakta, insulator = kihami, semiconductor = nusukondakta, superconductor = superkondakta; check these with a Kiswahili teacher), let pairs explain first in Kiswahili or their home language and then in English, and give the frame 'The bulb was ___ with ___, so ___ is a ___.'
records.why: The sequence has no language supports. English learners need the key words (conductor, insulator, semiconductor, superconductor) before they are used in Lessons 2 to 7, and Kiswahili first-language talk helps reasoning. The Kiswahili terms are suggestions I cannot verify, so the teacher must confirm or replace them with the words used locally.
records.group_headline: Added language supports (Kiswahili term suggestions, home-language talk, sentence frame) and more than one way to show understanding; the Kiswahili terms need a teacher to confirm

records.old: Do not correct models; instead ask 'What evidence supports that?'
records.new: Do not correct models; instead ask 'What evidence supports that?' Offer more than one way to show the model: a drawing, an arrangement of objects (for example beans for electrons), or an oral explanation to a partner or the teacher. Learners with low vision can use thick markers or tactile counters, and learners who find writing hard can dictate their 'what my model says' sentence.
records.why: No accommodation or alternative way to show understanding is given in the lessons; this adds short, practical options in the lesson where the first model is made.

records.old: Learners then compare it with their draft and revise.
records.new: Learners then compare it with their draft and revise. Learners who find extended writing hard may give the Final Explanation aloud to the teacher or a partner, or as a labelled diagram with a spoken explanation; first drafts may be in Kiswahili.
records.why: The Final Explanation is written. This gives a second way to show understanding for learners with writing difficulties or English as an additional language.

records.old: Resolve any odd result (for example a dull bulb with a flat cell) by asking the group to retest rather than dismissing it.
records.new: Resolve any odd result (for example a dull bulb with a flat cell) by asking the group to retest rather than dismissing it. Low-cost substitutes: take cells and 3 V bulbs from old torches, use stripped cable for the plastic strip, a ruler for dry wood, and a smooth-edged glass slide or bottle piece (checked by the teacher) for glass; any 1N400x rectifier diode (1N4001 to 1N4007) works in place of the 1N4007. If kits are fewer than groups, run stations of 6 to 8 learners that rotate.
records.why: Materials are listed but no low-cost substitutes or large-class option are given. The 1N4001 to 1N4007 diodes are all silicon rectifier diodes with the same one-way behaviour at 3 V, so the substitution is safe.

Lesson 5 depends on an offline PhET simulation 'on conductivity and energy bands' that lets learners set the gap, raise temperature and add phosphorus or boron, and the text says 'choose a metal if the simulation allows'. value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: uses accurate results from the bulb test and resistivity, gap and Tc values with correct units and the correct order of materials, and adds a comparison of his or her own (for example the silicon-to-copper ratio).
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: uses accurate results from the bulb test and resistivity, gap and Tc values with correct units and the correct order of materials.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: uses some evidence and numbers correctly, but units, order or results are missing or contain slips.

value.criterion: Scientific explanation using the band model
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: clearly explains conductors, insulators, semiconductors, temperature effects, doping and p-n junctions using energy gaps, free electrons and holes, and links the explanation to a new situation.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: explains conductors, insulators, semiconductors, doping and p-n junctions using energy gaps, free electrons and holes, with only small gaps in reasoning.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: describes what happens but gives only part of the why, or confuses ideas such as n-type and p-type.

value.criterion: Correct use of terms and conventions
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: uses conductor, insulator, semiconductor, superconductor, forward-biased and reverse-biased correctly throughout and always says insulators allow almost no current.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: uses the terms correctly with one or two mix-ups, and says insulators allow almost no current.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: often mixes terms or claims insulators allow no current at all.

value.criterion: Connection to Kenyan contexts and the Driving Question
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: links the answer to Mr Otieno's wiring and at least two Kenyan cases and answers both safety and efficiency fully.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: links the answer to Mr Otieno's wiring and at least one other Kenyan case and answers the Driving Question for safety and efficiency.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: links to wiring only, or answers the Driving Question in part.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: clearly describes how the class model changed from Lesson 1 and why, in well-organised sentences.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: describes how the class model changed and writes clearly most of the time.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: mentions model change only briefly, or writing is hard to follow.

records.why: The old descriptors were labelled Excellent, Proficient and Developing, but the CBE levels are Exceeds, Meets and Approaches Expectations (and Below Expectations). Descriptors now name the level and are written as a clear step up from level to level. The Meets descriptor for the Kenyan-context criterion was also tightened so the levels differ by quality, not only by count of cases.
